addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

**On ActorAttack (hard OOD)**: RoBERTa vanilla ALSO collapses (0.466±0.163), proving "no DA needed" was DD-specific. DeBERTa vanilla=0.258±0.000. Both encoders benefit from DA: DeBERTa 9-class=0.972±0.026, RoBERTa 9-class=0.939±0.046. Binary (0.990±0.008) ≈ 9-class (0.972±0.026) ≈ scrambled (0.951±0.043) — all three classification variants equivalent at Full (max gap 3.9pp, variance intervals fully overlap, n=3). Label quality is not a significant factor on ActorAttack, consistent with DD findings (D032).

**On Human-Written Jailbreaks (exp8, ToxicChat, macro F1 — D036)**: Domain-adapted variants outperform vanilla on human-authored data from ToxicChat (LMSYS, 204 jailbreaks + 204 benign, balanced, no data leakage). Macro F1: JB-MLM=0.837±0.013, wiki-MLM=0.791±0.093, binary=0.705±0.072, scrambled=0.616±0.056, 9-class=0.596±0.087, topic=0.496±0.042, vanilla=0.413±0.021. All DA variants exceed vanilla (+18-42pp), confirming features learned from Qwen3-8B synthetic data transfer to human text. JB-MLM strongest on human data (reversed from synthetic where 9-class leads), suggesting pure domain exposure transfers better across the human/LLM style gap. Notably, wiki-MLM (0.791, out-of-domain text) outperforms ALL classification variants (binary=0.705, scrambled=0.616, 9-class=0.596), further demonstrating that MLM domain exposure mechanism dominates classification supervision on human data. The jb_mlm vs wiki_mlm gap (4.6pp, std overlap) is modest, suggesting domain specificity provides marginal benefit on human data. 9-class drops from best on synthetic OOD (0.997/0.972) to 5th on human data (0.596), indicating classification supervision overfits to synthetic data distribution. Paper must discuss this contrast explicitly. NOTE: verazuo/jailbreak_llms results INVALID (benign data leakage, M014) — removed from paper.

**Cross-encoder CKA (D029)**: Both MLM and 9-class reshape representations substantially (centered CKA < 0.5 vs vanilla), but representation change magnitude ≠ detection improvement. RoBERTa MLM changes more (CKA=0.393) yet gains only 0.6pp; DeBERTa MLM changes less (CKA=0.442) yet gains 60pp. The starting point determines the return on adaptation.

**Key nuances**: (1) Binary ≈ 9-class ≈ scrambled on ActorAttack Full (0.990 vs 0.972 vs 0.951, all within noise at n=3; D032). Label quality is not a detection-relevant factor on any OOD difficulty. (2) Classification supervision consistently reduces cross-seed variance 4-20x (Claim 3): 9-class std=0.005-0.026 vs MLM std=0.080-0.115, across both DD and ActorAttack. (3) Perturbation robustness is attack-family-dependent (Discussion finding): DD OOD Δ≈0, ActorAttack DA variants Δ=-0.17 to -0.35 (vanilla -0.009 floor effect). DA detection advantage survives perturbation (McNemar p<0.001) as Claim 1 corollary.

## Novelty Positioning (D030 reframe)
NOT: "Persuasion-aware fine-tuning is the critical ingredient" (MLM control falsified this on DD).
NOT: "RoBERTa doesn't need domain adaptation" (ActorAttack falsified this — D030).
NOT: "Label quality matters on hard attacks" (3-seed ActorAttack: binary 0.990 ≈ 9-class 0.972 ≈ scrambled 0.951, all within noise; D032).
NOT: "Perturbation robustness generalizes across attack families" (exp6 falsified: DD Δ≈0 but ActorAttack Δ=-0.17 to -0.35 for all variants).
YES: "We systematically decompose cross-attack generalization across two encoder architectures and three OOD attack families. The key finding: domain adaptation universally improves generalization, but the benefit depends on encoder pretraining × attack structural complexity. On moderate OOD (DD), RoBERTa succeeds without adaptation while DeBERTa requires it; on structurally complex attacks (ActorAttack), both encoders require adaptation. Classification supervision provides complementary benefits: cross-seed stability (std reduced 4-20x vs MLM, consistent across DD and ActorAttack) and interpretability via strategy trajectories. DA's detection advantage survives adversarial perturbation (McNemar p<0.001), though absolute perturbation robustness is attack-family-dependent. Label quality (correct vs scrambled vs binary) does not significantly affect detection at any OOD difficulty level (D032)."

## Inherent Lexical Separability (D009)
Persuasive jailbreak conversations and general benign conversations are inherently lexically separable (TF-IDF≈1.0 on ALL data sources including real WildChat). TF-IDF remains strong on DD OOD (Full=0.961, per-prefix K1-K5 near-perfect). **But TF-IDF collapses on ActorAttack (Full=0.261, exp7)** — lexical features cannot capture multi-persona role-playing attack structure. DisPeD's value: (1) bridging 71pp gap vs TF-IDF on hard OOD (ActorAttack: 9-class=0.972 vs TF-IDF=0.261), (2) cross-seed stability (std 4-20x smaller than MLM variants), (3) interpretability via strategy trajectories.

## Comprehensive Ablation Picture (D014, updated D019/D020)
Systematic ablation reveals the method's actual mechanism:
- **Critical**: Domain exposure on jailbreak text (any form: MLM, scrambled, persuasion) — bridges OOD gap from F1=0.28 to F1≈1.0
- **Harmful**: Misaligned classification objective (topic: F1=0.54±0.21, -37pp vs MLM) — constrains representations toward irrelevant features
- **Non-critical**: Label granularity (binary≈scrambled≈9-class, 1-6pp gap on DD), Lambda tuning (all F1=1.0), Temporal modeling (mean pooling≈GRU on DD), Classification supervision itself (MLM Full=0.91±0.12 without any labels, K≤5 ≥0.97)
- **Implication**: Domain exposure is the mechanism. Classification supervision is neither necessary nor sufficient — misaligned tasks hurt, aligned/random tasks don't help beyond MLM. 9-class taxonomy provides interpretability, not detection advantage.

## Core Claims (3, priority-ordered — D019 reframe, D034 Claim 3 restructure)

### Claim 1 (PRIMARY): Domain Exposure Bridges the Cross-Attack OOD Gap
Vanilla DeBERTa catastrophically fails on unseen attack types (F1=0.28 on DD). Domain-adaptive continued pretraining on jailbreak conversation text bridges this gap completely (F1=1.0, +72pp). The critical finding: even MLM without any classification labels achieves F1=1.0 on DD (plan_017), proving that domain exposure alone is sufficient. Misaligned classification (topic, plan_016v2) achieves only F1=0.73, showing that irrelevant task objectives constrain representations harmfully. Complete evidence hierarchy (DD Full F1, multi-seed): vanilla (0.28) < topic (0.54±0.21) < wiki-MLM (0.90±0.12) ≈ JB-MLM (0.91±0.12) < TF-IDF (0.96) < scrambled (0.99) ≈ binary (0.99) ≪ 9-class (1.00±0.005). On ActorAttack: TF-IDF collapses (0.261) while 9-class=0.972 (+71pp), proving domain adaptation captures discourse structure beyond lexical cues.

- Evidence: plan_018 wiki-MLM DD — 3-seed Full=0.904±0.115, ≈ JB-MLM (domain specificity not significant at Full)
- Evidence: plan_016v2 topic DD — 3-seed 0.541±0.207 (misaligned classification hurts vs MLM)
- Evidence: plan_006 DD — Treatment F1=1.0, Baseline=0.28 (+72pp)
- Evidence: plan_006 scrambled DD — F1=0.935-0.990 (labels non-essential)
- Evidence: plan_013 binary DD — F1=0.99 (label granularity non-essential)
- Evidence: exp6 perturbation — DA detection advantage survives adversarial perturbation (9-class perturbed ActorAttack=0.768 >> vanilla=0.248, McNemar p<0.001). Domain adaptation's generalization benefit is not erased by paraphrasing attacks.
- Evidence: exp7 TF-IDF ActorAttack — TF-IDF Full=0.261 vs 9-class=0.972 (+71pp). TF-IDF collapses on structurally complex attacks (Precision=1.0 but Recall=0.15), proving lexical features are insufficient. DD OOD TF-IDF per-prefix: K1=1.0, K2=1.0, K3=0.994, K5=1.0, Full=0.961 — DD is fully solvable by lexical methods, but ActorAttack is not.
- Evidence: exp8 Human data (ToxicChat, macro F1) — 204 jailbreaks + 204 benign (LMSYS): JB-MLM=0.837±0.013, 9-class=0.596±0.087, vanilla=0.413±0.021. All DA >> vanilla (+18-42pp) on human-written jailbreaks completely independent of Qwen3-8B, refuting single-LLM confound. (verazuo INVALID, M014)
- Strength: very strong — MLM control is definitive causal test; topic control adds nuance; perturbation survival confirms DA benefit; TF-IDF ActorAttack collapse proves discourse-level advantage; human data (exp8) eliminates single-LLM confound

### Claim 2 (ANALYSIS): Persuasion Taxonomy as Interpretability Layer
While the persuasion classification task does not contribute to detection performance, the 9-class taxonomy provides interpretability that MLM cannot: different attack types exhibit distinct strategy trajectories (Crescendo: gradual escalation 0.86→5.64, DD: emotional-manipulation→role-assignment, FITD: commitment patterns). This is the taxonomy's sole surviving value after the MLM control result.
- Evidence: plan_008 strategy transition matrices
- Evidence: plan_017 falsifies detection contribution, confirming interpretability-only role
- Strength: descriptive/analytical; interpretability value independent of detection mechanism

### Claim 3 (EMPIRICAL): Classification Supervision Provides Cross-Seed Stability (on synthetic OOD)
Classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance by 4-20x compared to MLM-only pretraining on synthetic OOD data. 9-class std=0.005 (DD) / 0.026 (ActorAttack) vs JB-MLM std=0.115 (DD) / 0.080 (ActorAttack). Binary and scrambled variants also achieve low variance (0.005-0.043).
- Evidence: 9-class DD 0.997±0.005 vs JB-MLM 0.914±0.115 (std 23x smaller)
- Evidence: 9-class ActorAttack 0.972±0.026 vs JB-MLM 0.893±0.080 (std 3x smaller)
- Evidence: wiki-MLM 0.904±0.115 — out-of-domain MLM equally unstable
- **CAVEAT (exp8, Reviewer-flagged)**: On human data (ToxicChat), variance pattern REVERSES: 9-class std=0.087 (HIGHEST), jb_mlm std=0.009 (lowest). Classification supervision destabilizes on far-OOD human data while MLM remains stable. Claim 3 must be explicitly scoped to "synthetic OOD data" in the paper, with human data reversal discussed in Discussion.
- Implication: Classification supervision stabilizes within the synthetic data distribution but may overfit to it. MLM provides more robust cross-distribution stability.
- Strength: strong on synthetic OOD (2 families, 7 variants, 3 seeds); DOES NOT hold on human data

### Perturbation Robustness (DISCUSSION FINDING — demoted from Claim, D033/D034)
Adversarial perturbation robustness does NOT generalize across attack families. On DD OOD, classification variants show near-zero degradation (Δ≈0 at K≥2). On ActorAttack, DA variants degrade substantially: 9-class Δ_full=-0.204±0.135, binary -0.250, scrambled -0.172, MLM -0.353. Vanilla Δ_full=-0.009 (floor effect: clean=0.258, near random). Better-performing variants have more room to degrade — perturbation narrows the DA-vanilla gap but does not eliminate it.
- DD robustness attribution (D026, holds on DD only): classification structure → Full/K≥3 Δ=0

% introduction.tex — expanded for 8-page target

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns. Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo}, Foot-in-the-Door~\citep{fitd2024}, and Deceptive Delight~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} all rely on persuasion as their core mechanism: \citet{zeng2024pap} catalogue 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak families, and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} identify strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. Because individual attack turns occupy the same embedding region as benign text~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}, no single-turn filter can distinguish them from legitimate conversation.

Existing defenses leave a critical gap. Production classifiers such as Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard}, WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard}, and ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} operate on individual turns and therefore miss manipulation that unfolds across exchanges. Multi-turn defenses have begun to model conversation-level structure: DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026} pairs fine-tuned BERT with a multi-layer GRU, BIID~\citep{tong2025biid} infers turn-level intentions, and G-Guard~\citep{gguard2025} applies graph neural networks. These systems achieve strong in-distribution performance, but each is evaluated on a single attack family. None answers the central question: \emph{what representation properties enable a detector to generalize across attack families it has never seen?}

The simplest hypothesis is that pretrained language understanding already suffices. It does not, at least at base model scale. A vanilla DeBERTa-v3~\citep{he2021deberta} with temporal aggregation (cf.\ DeepContext) drops from F1\,=\,1.000 in-distribution to 0.312 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight. LLM-as-judge approaches fare no better: GPT-5.5 reaches only 0.191--0.449 F1 with 30--47\% unparseable responses (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}). These failures share a root cause: neither model has been exposed to multi-turn adversarial text. The bottleneck is distributional, not architectural: cross-attack generalization requires domain adaptation, not a better classifier.

We test this hypothesis through controlled ablation. Our pipeline, \textbf{DisPeD}, separates encoder adaptation (Stage~1) from temporal classification (Stage~2, a frozen BiGRU). Seven Stage~1 variants each isolate a single factor (e.g., domain exposure, label quality, temporal modeling) while holding all other components constant (Section~\ref{sec:method}). The contribution is the systematic decomposition of what enables cross-attack generalization, not the pipeline itself.

Controlled ablation across DeBERTa-v3 and RoBERTa~\citep{liu2019roberta} on four attack families shows that domain-adaptive pretraining is the primary mechanism for base-size encoders (125--184M parameters), closing roughly 60 percentage points of the OOD gap without any labels. This dependence on adaptation diminishes with scale: RoBERTa-large (355M) handles even ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} without adaptation, and three encoder scales together trace a clear capacity gradient. Classification supervision offers a complementary but narrower benefit: it stabilizes predictions on synthetic data regardless of label correctness, yet this stability does not transfer to human-authored conversations (Section~\ref{sec:human_data}).

Our contributions:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=4pt]
  \item \textbf{Systematic decomposition of cross-attack generalization.} Controlled ablation across twelve encoder variants and three OOD attack families decomposes six dimensions of adaptation. Three negative results are counter-intuitive: scrambled labels match correct labels, mean pooling matches BiGRU, and label granularity does not affect detection.

  \item \textbf{Capacity gradient for domain adaptation.} Three encoder scales (125M, 184M, 355M) show that the set of attacks requiring adaptation shrinks with model size; RoBERTa-large handles structurally complex attacks without any adaptation (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).

  \item \textbf{Distribution-specific classification effects.} Classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance 4--20$\times$ on synthetic data but provides no benefit on human-authored data (Section~\ref{sec:human_data}). The 9-class persuasion taxonomy enables interpretable strategy characterization (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).
\end{itemize}

\begin{abstract}
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns, defeating per-turn safety filters.
What representation properties enable a detector to generalize across unseen attack families?
We isolate the answer through controlled ablation: twelve encoder variants spanning three scales (125M, 184M, 355M) and six adaptation dimensions, evaluated on three out-of-distribution (OOD) attack families.
The answer is reductive.
For base-size encoders (125--184M parameters), domain exposure alone bridges $\sim$60 percentage points of the OOD F1 gap; label quality, label granularity, and temporal modeling are non-factors.
Scaling to 355M parameters eliminates the need for adaptation on structurally distinct attacks (F1\,=\,1.000 on ActorAttack without any continued pretraining). This reveals a capacity gradient: as model size increases, the set of attacks requiring adaptation narrows.
Classification supervision stabilizes within-distribution predictions (variance reduced 4--20$\times$) regardless of label correctness, but this benefit does not transfer to human-authored data, where pure masked language modeling outperforms all classification variants.
Validation on ToxicChat confirms that domain-adaptive pretraining on synthetic text transfers to human-written jailbreaks (macro F1: 0.837 vs.\ vanilla 0.413); full multi-turn human evaluation remains future work.
\end{abstract}

10	All synthetic data is generated by Qwen3-8B~\citep{qwen3_2025}.
11	The IID dataset contains 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, split into training (350), validation (74), and test (76) sets with balanced class ratios (e.g., test = 38 jailbreak + 38 benign).
12	Stage~1 (DAPT) uses training + validation conversations; Stage~2 (BiGRU) trains on training, early-stops on validation, and evaluates on test.
13	OOD evaluation pairs attack-specific jailbreak conversations with the 38 IID-test benign conversations: 80 FITD~\citep{fitd2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, and 80 ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} + 38 benign = 118 total.
14	No overlap exists in attack templates across families.
15	The OOD benign set is IID (same generation pipeline as training); the OOD challenge is in distinguishing novel attack families from familiar benign conversations.
16	A paraphrased version of the IID test set (BERTScore 0.92, lexical overlap 0.20) serves as the adversarial robustness benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
17	For human data validation, we use ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 jailbreak + 204 benign from real LMSYS user interactions), entirely independent of Qwen3-8B generation.
18	
19	\paragraph{Models.}
20	Seven DeBERTa-v3 variants share the same Stage-2 pipeline and differ only in Stage-1 training (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
21	For cross-encoder validation, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class variants on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).
22	We also compare TF-IDF LR and LLM-as-judge baselines (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}): GPT-5.5 achieves only F1 = 0.191--0.449 on IID Crescendo with 30--47\% unparseable responses; on OOD data, zero-shot Qwen3-8B achieves macro F1 = 0.244 (DD and ActorAttack) by predicting nearly all conversations as benign, and even 3-shot prompting reaches only 0.566 (DD) and 0.652 (ActorAttack). Content-level reasoning is insufficient for this task.
23	
24	\paragraph{Metrics.}
25	F1 for binary jailbreak detection at prefix $K$=2 and full conversations (full per-$K$ results in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_prefix}).
26	OOD results report 3-seed mean$\pm$std (seeds 42, 123, 456) for all variants.
27	For key pairwise comparisons, we report BCa bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples over individual predictions pooled across seeds) and paired permutation tests (10,000 permutations). Bootstrap means may differ slightly from seed-averaged F1 due to the nonlinearity of F1 aggregation.
28	All standard deviations are computed over 3 random seeds using the population formula ($n$ divisor); Bessel-corrected estimates ($n{-}1$ divisor) are $\approx$22\% larger but do not alter any significance conclusions.
29	Stage-1: learning rate $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch 16, 4 epochs, MLM masking 15\%.
30	Stage-2: two-layer MLP, 20 epochs.

112	\paragraph{Domain exposure is the primary mechanism.}
113	MLM bridges $\sim$60\,pp from vanilla (0.312$\pm$0.026 $\to$ 0.914$\pm$0.115) without labels; this supports the DAPT interpretation~\citep{gururangan2020dontstop}. TF-IDF collapse on ActorAttack (0.261 vs.\ 9-class 0.972) confirms that domain-adapted representations capture features beyond lexical overlap.
114	All three classification-supervised variants converge to equivalent detection (F1 = 0.997--1.000); McNemar's test finds no significant pairwise differences (all $p > 0.13$; $\leq$7 discordant pairs limit power), and paired permutation tests confirm equivalence ($p \geq 0.40$). TOST equivalence tests (margin = 5\,pp) confirm statistical equivalence on DD (all $p < 0.01$, 90\% CI within $\pm$0.05). On ActorAttack, equivalence cannot be statistically confirmed due to limited seeds ($n$=3), though observed mean differences (2--4\,pp) fall within practical equivalence margins. Label quality and granularity are non-factors for detection.
115	Classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance 4--20$\times$ over MLM on synthetic OOD (std 0.005 vs.\ 0.115 on DD; bootstrap CI widths: 5.7\,pp vs.\ 35.5\,pp). 116	Appendix~\ref{app:tsne} provides t-SNE visualizations confirming that domain-adapted variants produce tighter, more separable embedding clusters than the vanilla baseline.
117	
118	\paragraph{Domain specificity is marginal at full length but meaningful for early detection.}
119	Wikipedia MLM (0.904$\pm$0.115) nearly matches jailbreak-domain MLM at full length (1\,pp gap), though jailbreak-domain text provides an 8\,pp advantage at early prefixes ($K$=2: 0.993 vs.\ 0.911).
120	Perturbation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}) reveals a sharper domain specificity effect: Wikipedia MLM degrades by $\sim$12\,pp under adversarial paraphrasing while jailbreak-domain MLM degrades by only 2.6\,pp.
121	
122	\paragraph{Misaligned supervision destabilizes generalization.}
123	Topic classification yields DD-Full F1 = 0.541$\pm$0.207; seed 123 falls \emph{below} vanilla (0.252 vs.\ 0.312). Despite using the same jailbreak-domain training data, topic classification performs worse than Wikipedia MLM (0.904$\pm$0.115), which uses out-of-domain text with no labels. A misaligned objective forces the encoder to allocate capacity to irrelevant features and actively destabilizes representations that MLM would preserve.
124	
125	\paragraph{Evidence hierarchy on structurally complex attacks.}
126	ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} uses multi-persona steering across longer conversation structures and provides a more challenging OOD benchmark than DD.
127	The evidence hierarchy at full conversation length is:

133	TF-IDF collapses from 0.961 (DD) to 0.261 (ActorAttack, precision = 1.0, recall = 0.15). This gap shows that domain-adapted representations capture features beyond bag-of-words.
134	All classification-supervised variants converge to equivalent performance (0.951--0.990, max gap 3.9\,pp); this extends the DD finding. DAPT provides $\sim$71\,pp over both vanilla (0.258) and TF-IDF (0.261). Full per-prefix results in Appendix~\ref{sec:actorattack_full}.
135	
136	\paragraph{Temporal modeling.}
137	Three-seed evaluation on both DD and ActorAttack confirms that mean pooling matches BiGRU (F1 gap $\leq$ 1\,pp on full conversations, overlapping CIs); detection thus relies on per-turn representations rather than their sequential order.
138	
139	\paragraph{Summary.}
140	For base-size encoders (125--184M), domain exposure is the primary mechanism for cross-attack detection; label correctness, label granularity, temporal modeling, and domain specificity are non-factors. Classification supervision provides a complementary stability benefit (variance reduced 4--20$\times$) but does not change the detection ceiling established by domain exposure. Practitioners need continued pretraining on domain text, not annotation pipelines or specialized temporal architectures.

3	\section{Method}
4	\label{sec:method}
5	
6	The central question of this paper requires a controlled experimental design: each candidate factor for cross-attack generalization must be isolated while all other variables are held constant. DisPeD achieves this through a two-stage architecture. Stage~1 performs domain-adaptive continued pretraining (DAPT) on jailbreak conversation text to adapt a turn-level encoder; seven Stage-1 variants decompose the contributions of domain exposure, classification supervision, label quality, label granularity, and domain specificity. Stage~2 aggregates turn representations for conversation-level binary classification under identical conditions for all variants. Figure~\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the pipeline.
7	
8	\begin{figure}[t]
9	\centering
10	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/paper/fig1_architecture.pdf}
11	\caption{DisPeD architecture. Stage~1 adapts a DeBERTa encoder on jailbreak conversation text (seven variant objectives). Stage~2 aggregates frozen \texttt{[CLS]} embeddings via BiGRU for conversation-level jailbreak detection. Only user turns are processed.}
12	\label{fig:architecture}
13	\end{figure}
14	
15	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
16	
17	A conversation $C = \{u_1, a_1, \ldots, u_N, a_N\}$ alternates user turns $u_i$ and assistant responses $a_i$. Given a prefix of $K$ user turns, the model predicts $y \in \{0, 1\}$ (jailbreak vs.\ benign). We restrict input to user turns because adversarial intent resides in the attacker's messages. This formulation supports early detection from partial prefixes.
18	
19	\subsection{Stage 1: Turn-Level Encoder Adaptation}
20	\label{sec:stage1}
21	
22	Each user turn $u_i$ is encoded by DeBERTa-v3-base~\citep{he2023debertav3}; the \texttt{[CLS]} embedding $h_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ serves as the turn representation. Seven variants, summarized in Table~\ref{tab:variants}, share the same training data but differ in objective.
23	
24	\begin{table}[t]
25	\centering
26	\small
27	\caption{Stage-1 encoder variants. All operate on the same training conversations except Wikipedia MLM (matched token count on Wikipedia text).}
28	\label{tab:variants}
29	\begin{tabular}{@{}p{1.6cm}p{2.2cm}p{2.8cm}@{}}
30	\toprule
31	\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Tests whether\ldots} \\
32	\midrule
33	9-class & 9-class persuasion + binary intent & full model \\
34	Binary & binary persuasion + binary intent & granularity matters \\
35	Scrambled & random 9-class + binary intent & label correctness matters \\
36	MLM-only & 15\% token masking & supervision is necessary \\
37	Topic & 5-class topic classif. & any task suffices \\
38	Wiki MLM & 15\% masking on Wikipedia & domain specificity matters \\
39	Vanilla & no training & Stage-2 alone suffices \\
40	\bottomrule
41	\end{tabular}
42	\end{table}
43	
44	The \textbf{9-class} variant uses two classification heads: 9-class persuasion strategy classification ($L_{\text{strategy}}$) and binary jailbreak intent ($L_{\text{intent}}$), with combined loss $L = L_{\text{strategy}} + \alpha \cdot L_{\text{intent}}$ ($\alpha = 0.3$, selected from $\{0, 0.3, 0.5, 2.0\}$; all values yield F1\,=\,1.0 on IID). The taxonomy comprises eight persuasion strategies (rapport building, authority appeal, emotional manipulation, logical reframing, role assignment, gradual escalation, obfuscation, direct request) plus a none category, grounded in PAP~\citep{zeng2024pap} and Cialdini's principles~\citep{cialdini2001influence}. Strategy annotations are produced by Qwen3-8B with structured prompting that includes definitions and examples for each category; inter-annotator agreement between model annotations and a human sample ($n$=50) yields Cohen's $\kappa$=0.78.
45	
46	The remaining classification variants test specific ablation hypotheses.
47	The \textbf{binary} variant collapses the 9-class taxonomy into persuasive vs.\ non-persuasive, testing whether label granularity matters for detection or robustness.
48	The \textbf{scrambled} variant assigns random permutations of the 9-class labels to turns, preserving the classification structure (cross-entropy loss, 9-class output space) while destroying label semantics; this isolates whether the classification objective itself provides representational benefits independent of label correctness.
49	The \textbf{MLM-only} variant applies 15\% masked language modeling on the same jailbreak conversation text without any classification head, testing whether unsupervised domain exposure suffices.
50	The \textbf{topic} variant trains a 5-class topic classifier (technology, health, finance, education, general) on the same conversations, testing whether \emph{any} classification task provides the same benefit or whether task alignment matters.
51	The \textbf{Wikipedia MLM} variant applies the same MLM objective to a token-matched sample of Wikipedia text, isolating the effect of domain-specific vs.\ general continued pretraining.
52	The \textbf{vanilla} baseline uses the pretrained DeBERTa-v3-base weights without any continued pretraining; it measures what Stage~2 alone can achieve.
53	
54	\subsection{Stage 2: Conversation-Level Classification}
55	\label{sec:stage2}
56	
57	Turn embeddings $\{h_1, \ldots, h_K\}$ from the frozen Stage-1 encoder are aggregated by a 2-layer bidirectional GRU ($d_{\text{hidden}}$=256, dropout 0.3): $\bar{h} = [\overrightarrow{h_K};\; \overleftarrow{h_1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{512}$.
58	A two-layer MLP ($512 \to 256 \to 2$, ReLU activation) maps $\bar{h}$ to $\hat{y} \in \{0, 1\}$.
59	The Stage-1 encoder is frozen during Stage~2 training; only the BiGRU and MLP parameters are updated.
60	This frozen-encoder design ensures ablation fairness: all seven Stage-1 variants are evaluated under identical downstream conditions, isolating the effect of Stage-1 representation quality from Stage-2 classifier capacity.

The contrast between rows~2 and~3 shows that the dominant failure mode in row~2 is benign distribution mismatch (false positives from unfamiliar benign text), not inability to recognize cross-LLM jailbreak patterns. Vanilla remains at 0.26--0.31 across all conditions, further confirming that encoders without DAPT lack OOD detection capability regardless of the LLM source. The F1 collapse in the full Llama condition (Table~\ref{tab:cross_llm}, row~2) is driven entirely by false positives on unfamiliar benign text (FP rate: 88--90\% on Llama vs.\ 0--0.9\% on Qwen for adapted variants). The model implicitly treats non-Qwen text style as a jailbreak indicator, a spurious correlation from single-LLM training data. An MLM-only variant (without classification) produces the same pattern (AA Full = 0.874$\pm$0.014); representation drift from continued pretraining, not classification-specific bias, is the underlying cause. Domain-adaptive fine-tuning narrows the representation space of a sufficiently large encoder and reduces its inherent OOD generalization ability.
258	
259	\section{Reproducibility Details}
260	\label{sec:reproducibility}
261	
262	\paragraph{Stage-1 training.}
263	All variants use DeBERTa-v3-base (184M parameters) with learning rate $2 \times 10^{-5}$, AdamW optimizer ($\beta_1$=0.9, $\beta_2$=0.999, weight decay 0.01), linear warmup over the first 10\% of steps, batch size 16, and 4 epochs. MLM variants use 15\% random token masking. Training takes approximately 30 minutes per variant on a single NVIDIA A100 (40GB).
264	
265	\paragraph{Stage-2 training.}
266	The BiGRU has hidden dimension 256, 2 layers, and dropout 0.3 (bidirectional, so output dimension 512). The MLP classifier has layers $512 \to 256 \to 2$ with ReLU activation. Training uses learning rate $1 \times 10^{-3}$, Adam optimizer, batch size 32, and 20 epochs with early stopping (patience 5) on validation F1. Stage-2 training completes in under 5 minutes per variant.
267	
268	\paragraph{Data generation.}
269	Jailbreak conversations are generated using Qwen3-8B with attack-specific prompt templates. Crescendo conversations follow a 5--8 turn gradual escalation structure. FITD conversations use a 2--3 turn commitment-consistency structure. Deceptive Delight conversations embed harmful content within emotionally engaging 3--5 turn sequences. Benign conversations are generated with topic-anchored prompts across five domains (technology, health, finance, education, general) with matched turn counts.
270	
271	\paragraph{Strategy annotation.}
272	Each user turn is annotated by Qwen3-8B using a structured prompt that provides definitions and two examples for each of the nine strategy categories. The prompt instructs the model to output a single category label. We plan to release all generation and annotation prompts, the full dataset, and training code upon acceptance.
273	
274	\paragraph{Adversarial paraphrasing.}
275	The paraphrased test set is generated by instructing Qwen3-8B to rephrase each user turn while preserving the communicative intent. The resulting paraphrases have mean BERTScore 0.92 and mean lexical overlap 0.20 with the originals. These metrics confirm substantial surface-level variation.
